name: Water
fact: Water has an unusually high heat capacity, so it warms slowly and soaks up the heat of a reaction.

name: Acetic acid
fact: Vinegar is about 5% acetic acid in water. Pure acetic acid freezes at 16.6 C.

name: Ethanol
fact: Ethanol burns with a pale blue flame that is hard to see in daylight.

name: Vegetable oil
fact: Oil floats on water because it is less dense, and the two do not mix because water molecules stick to each other far more than to oil.

name: Hydrogen peroxide
fact: The 6% bottle here is the strength sold as hair developer, the usual one for elephant toothpaste. It slowly falls apart into water and oxygen on its own.

name: Sugar
fact: Table sugar is sucrose. A cup of water dissolves about two cups of it.

name: Caramel
fact: Heat sugar past about 170 C and it sheds water and browns into hundreds of new flavour molecules.

name: Cornstarch
fact: Cornstarch in water makes oobleck, a fluid that turns solid when you hit it.

name: Dish soap
fact: Soap molecules line every bubble so the film does not burst. A squirt of soap turns a fizz into a mountain of foam.

name: Yeast
fact: Yeast carries catalase, an enzyme that breaks hydrogen peroxide apart thousands of times a second.

name: Universal indicator
fact: Universal indicator is a blend of dyes: red in acid, green when neutral, purple in strong alkali.

name: Blue food colouring
fact: A single drop of food colouring is enough to tint a litre of water.

name: Table salt
fact: Salt dissolves to about 36 g per 100 mL of water, and it barely changes with temperature.

name: Baking soda
fact: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate. Acid or heat makes it give up carbon dioxide, which is what raises a cake.

name: Washing soda
fact: Sodium carbonate, or soda ash, is one of the three ingredients of ordinary glass.

name: Sodium acetate
fact: Sodium acetate is the 'hot ice' in reusable hand warmers.

name: Magnesium acetate
fact: Dissolving a reactive metal in an acid always leaves a salt of that metal behind.

name: Sodium ethoxide
fact: Sodium reacts with alcohol the way it does with water, only far more gently.

name: Sodium hydroxide
fact: Sodium hydroxide, or lye, is a strong base. It feels slippery because it is turning the oils in your skin into soap.

name: Potassium hydroxide
fact: Caustic potash. Soft soaps are made with it.

name: Lithium hydroxide
fact: Spacecraft use lithium hydroxide to scrub carbon dioxide out of the cabin air.

name: Slaked lime
fact: Calcium hydroxide barely dissolves, so it turns water milky. The clear part is called limewater.

name: Magnesium oxide
fact: The white ash left by burning magnesium melts at 2852 C, which is why it lines furnaces.

name: Iron sulfide
fact: Mix iron and sulfur and a magnet pulls them apart. Heat them and they become a new substance that no magnet can separate.

name: Copper oxide
fact: Hot copper turns black as it joins with oxygen from the air.

name: Rust
fact: Rust is iron oxide. Iron needs both oxygen and water to rust, and salt speeds it up.

name: Aluminium oxide
fact: A layer of this oxide a few atoms thick is all that stops aluminium from corroding. As a crystal it is ruby and sapphire.

name: Phosphorus pentoxide
fact: The dense white smoke from burning phosphorus grabs water so strongly that it is used to dry other chemicals.

name: Carbon dioxide
fact: Carbon dioxide is one and a half times heavier than air, so it pours downward and pools in low places.

name: Oxygen
fact: Oxygen does not burn. It makes everything else burn faster.

name: Hydrogen
fact: Hydrogen is 14 times lighter than air and burns in almost any mixture from 4% to 75%.

name: Sulfur dioxide
fact: The choking smell of a struck match is sulfur dioxide.

name: Sodium
fact: Sodium is soft enough to cut with a butter knife and light enough to float on water.

name: Potassium
fact: Potassium melts at 64 C and catches fire the moment it touches water.

name: Lithium
fact: Lithium is the lightest metal. It floats even on oil.

name: Calcium
fact: Your bones hold about a kilogram of calcium.

name: Magnesium
fact: Burning magnesium was the first camera flash.

name: Aluminium
fact: Aluminium was once worth more than gold. Now it wraps sandwiches.

name: Iron
fact: Iron is magnetic until 770 C, then it suddenly is not.

name: Copper
fact: Copper is one of very few metals that is not grey.

name: Gold
fact: Gold does not tarnish, rust or dissolve in ordinary acids. Almost nothing happens to it.

name: Mercury
fact: Mercury is so dense that iron and lead float on it.

name: Sulfur
fact: Molten sulfur is runny, then thick as syrup near 180 C, then runny again.

name: Red phosphorus
fact: Red phosphorus is on the striking strip of a matchbox, not on the match.

name: Silicon
fact: Silicon conducts better as it warms up, which is the opposite of a metal.

name: Carbon
fact: Charcoal, graphite and diamond are all pure carbon. Only the arrangement of the atoms differs.

name: Hydrochloric acid
fact: Hydrochloric acid is hydrogen chloride gas dissolved in water. Your stomach makes it to digest food.

name: Citric acid
fact: Citric acid is what makes lemons sour. It is a weak acid: only a small fraction of it splits into ions in water.

name: Sodium citrate
fact: Sodium citrate gives sports drinks and some sweets their tangy, salty taste.

name: Marble chips
fact: Marble, limestone and chalk are all calcium carbonate. Acid rain slowly dissolves marble statues for exactly this reason.

name: Calcium chloride
fact: Calcium chloride is spread on icy roads. It melts ice at far lower temperatures than table salt.

name: Magnesium chloride
fact: Magnesium chloride is pulled from sea water to make magnesium metal.

name: Iron(II) chloride
fact: Iron(II) salts are pale green in solution. Left in air they slowly turn rusty brown as they become iron(III).

name: Copper(II) chloride
fact: Copper chloride solution is blue-green. In a flame it burns a vivid blue-green, which is how fireworks get that colour.

name: Copper sulfate
fact: Copper sulfate crystals are deep blue because each copper ion holds five water molecules. Far more dissolves in hot water than cold, which makes it perfect for growing crystals.

name: Anhydrous copper sulfate
fact: Without its water, copper sulfate is a white powder. A single drop of water turns it blue again, so chemists use it to test for water.

name: Iron(II) sulfate
fact: Iron sulfate is pale green. Gardeners use it to green up lawns and kill moss.

name: Magnesium sulfate
fact: Magnesium sulfate is Epsom salt, the stuff people soak tired feet in.

name: Alum
fact: Alum grows clear eight-sided crystals. Ten times more of it dissolves in boiling water than in cold, so it crystallises beautifully as it cools.

name: Red cabbage juice
fact: Red cabbage contains anthocyanin dyes that change colour across the whole pH scale: red in acid, purple near neutral, then blue, green and yellow as it gets more alkaline.

name: Phenolphthalein
fact: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and neutral water, and turns bright pink above about pH 8.2. It is the classic indicator for titrations.
